item.title: Writing K2 Compiler Plugins: Type-Safe Validation and Resource Generation
item.content:encoded:
K2 Compiler Playbook

A step-by-step playbook to frontend FIR inspection and backend IR resource generation.

Most of what you find online about custom Kotlin compiler plugins is outdated or unhelpfully abstract. When I started building KAutoService, I spent two days digging through compiler source jars just to understand how K2 registers a basic class checker.

GitHub - JosephSanjaya/KAutoService: A Kotlin K2 compiler plugin that automatically registers service providers, serving as the native Kotlin successor to Java's AutoService.

This guide is the playbook I wish I had. We will build a native Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) compiler plugin that automates service registration without the performance overhead of traditional annotation processors.

In Java, registering services via ServiceLoader requires writing configuration files under META-INF/services/. Manually managing these files is error-prone. While Google's AutoService library automates this for Java, it relies on Java Annotation Processing (APT), which does not support Kotlin Multiplatform targets. KAutoService solves this problem by using a native Kotlin K2 compiler plugin to validate and generate service registry entries during compilation.

The Architecture of a K2 Compiler Plugin

K2 divides compilation into two separate phases. First, the Frontend Intermediate Representation (FIR) parses source code, resolves type symbols, and builds a semantic representation. This is the inspection phase. Next, the Backend Intermediate Representation (IR) takes this fully resolved semantic tree and generates platform-specific bytecode. This is the transformation phase.

To connect our logic to these phases, we register custom extensions. A single compiler plugin registrar exposes both entry points. Our registrar registers a FIR extension for compile-time validation and an IR extension for output file generation. This is defined in KAutoServicePluginRegistrar.kt.

class KAutoServicePluginRegistrar : CompilerPluginRegistrar() {
    override val supportsK2 = true
    override val pluginId = "io.github.josephsanjaya.kautoservice"

    override fun ExtensionStorage.registerExtensions(configuration: CompilerConfiguration) {
        val enabled = configuration.get(KAutoServiceConfigurationKeys.ENABLED, true)
        if (!enabled) return

        FirExtensionRegistrarAdapter.registerExtension(KAutoServiceFirRegistrar())
        IrGenerationExtension.registerExtension(KAutoServiceIrExtension(configuration))
    }
}

By returning true for supportsK2, the plugin notifies the compiler that it is fully compatible with the new K2 analysis engine.

Frontend Validation (FIR)

The Frontend Intermediate Representation (FIR) represents your code as a structured semantic tree. This tree contains fully resolved types and symbol descriptors, which makes it perfect for compile-time validation. Unlike old compiler analysis tools, FIR allows us to inspect classes and raise errors before any bytecode or files are generated.

Think of FIR as the compiler’s type checker. In KAutoService, we write a custom FirClassChecker to inspect classes annotated with @AutoService. We must enforce three rules:

  1. The target must be a class (not an interface or enum).
  2. The class must be concrete (not abstract or sealed).
  3. The class must implement the interface declared in the annotation.

We inspect the annotation values and call K2’s built-in type checker to verify the subtype relationship. The following snippet performs the subtype validation.

val serviceTypes = extractServiceTypes(annotation)
val classType = classSymbol.classId.constructClassLikeType(emptyArray(), false)
for (serviceType in serviceTypes) {
    val isSubtype = classType.isSubtypeOf(serviceType, context.session)
    if (!isSubtype) {
        val serviceName = serviceType.classId?.asSingleFqName().asString() ?: serviceType.toString()
        reportError("Service provider $className does not implement declared service interface $serviceName")
    }
}

The isSubtypeOf function queries K2's internal type system to confirm that the implementing class can be safely cast to the service interface.

Backend Resource Generation (IR)

Backend compilation transforms the validated syntax trees into platform assets. K2 represents compiled code as Intermediate Representation (IR) graphs, which provide a platform-agnostic view of the program structure. This phase creates files. Our extension runs a recursive traversal to gather target classes. Once collected, we locate the compiler output directory and write standard configuration files directly to the build folder.

In this stage, the compiler has already checked all rules in the FIR phase. This means we can safely assume that any class decorated with @AutoService is a valid service implementer.

We inspect the AST declarations to extract the implementation binary name and its service interfaces. This extraction is done in processClass.

private fun processClass(irClass: IrClass, servicesMap: MutableMap<String, MutableSet<String>>) {
    val annotation = irClass.annotations.find {
        it.type.classFqName == autoServiceFqn
    } ?: return
    val implName = getJvmBinaryName(irClass)
    val vararg = annotation.arguments[0] as? IrVararg ?: return
    vararg.elements.forEach { element ->
        val classRef = element as? IrClassReference ?: return@forEach
        val referencedClass = classRef.symbol.owner as? IrClass ?: return@forEach
        val serviceName = getJvmBinaryName(referencedClass)
        servicesMap.getOrPut(serviceName) { mutableSetOf() }.add(implName)
    }
}

By parsing the annotation argument as IrVararg containing IrClassReference elements, we resolve the underlying class declarations to fetch their fully-qualified binary names.

Operational Lessons

Custom compiler plugins require a shift in engineering mindset. We learned three core lessons during development that should guide any engineer building on K2.

  1. Separate inspection from transformation: FIR extensions must never modify code or write files. They exist to report errors. IR extensions do the heavy lifting of generating assets.
  2. Avoid fragile string comparison for types: K2 provides type-safe APIs like isSubtypeOf to verify class relationships correctly.
  3. Use MessageCollector for diagnostics: Printing to stdout is hard to trace in build logs. The compiler’s message collector surfaces warnings and errors cleanly.

Conclusion

K2 compiler plugins represent the future of Kotlin development. By moving checks to the compiler frontend, we eliminate runtime crashes and keep builds fast. Custom rules ensure our codebase stays safe.

item.title: 5 Low-Effort Wins Hidden in Your Backend Config
item.content:encoded:
Building a backend that performs well under real traffic doesn’t require a complex setup. But it does require a minimum baseline of things that most backends skip on the first pass: capping connections, compressing responses, protecting endpoints, handling failures from external services gracefully.

None of this is advanced. It’s the kind of low-effort, one-time configuration that sits quietly in the background and prevents the class of problems that only show up when traffic grows, or something external misbehaves. A third-party integration hangs and takes your whole server with it. A spike opens too many database connections, and suddenly nothing works. An endpoint gets hammered, and you have no idea until the database is on fire.

The five things below are that baseline. They take an hour to ship, and you’ll likely never think about them again. But you’ll definitely feel it when they’re missing.

Concepts apply to any backend stack, code examples are in Node.js.

1. Your JSON responses are traveling at full weight

Every API response goes over the wire at full size unless you tell it not to. For a typical JSON payload (a user profile, a list of items, some nested config), that might be 4–8 KB. Not alarming in isolation. But at a few hundred concurrent users, especially on mobile connections or across regions, you’re shipping a lot of bytes that compress down to almost nothing.

Gzip compression can reduce JSON payloads by 60–80%. The reason JSON compresses so well is structural: it’s full of repeated keys, predictable patterns, and whitespace. That’s exactly the kind of redundancy compression algorithms exploit. A 6 KB user object might come out as 900 bytes on the wire.

Most frameworks have a middleware or built-in option for this. In Express it’s the compression package. It negotiates encoding with the client via the Accept-Encoding header, falls back gracefully for clients that don't support it, and skips responses below a configurable size threshold (1 KB by default, which already filters out health checks and lightweight pings):

const compression = require('compression');
app.use(compression()); // place this before your routes

That said, compression is not always the right call. It adds CPU work on the server side, since each response has to be encoded before it goes out. For most JSON APIs this overhead is negligible, but if your server is already CPU-bound or you’re serving a very high request volume of small payloads, the tradeoff flips. In those scenarios, offloading compression to a reverse proxy (Nginx, a CDN, or an AWS ALB with compression enabled) is a better pattern. The proxy handles encoding while your application server stays focused on business logic. Similarly, for streaming responses or server-sent events, response compression should be disabled or bypassed, since compressing a stream in chunks reduces its effectiveness significantly.

For the majority of JSON APIs, though, this is the highest effort-to-impact ratio change on this list.

2. A slow third-party API can freeze your entire app

When a server makes an outbound network call and waits for the response, it’s holding resources: an open socket, a thread or event loop slot, potentially a database connection. If the downstream server never responds, that wait never ends. The request just sits there indefinitely, holding everything it acquired when it started.

A payment provider having a bad minute. An internal microservice deployed with a memory leak. A third-party API rate-limiting you silently instead of returning an error. Any of these can cause a cascade: one request hangs, then ten, then your worker pool fills up and new requests start failing too. The symptom looks like your app is broken, but your app is fine. It’s just waiting politely for something that will never come.

The fix is explicit timeouts on every external call. In Node.js, AbortController is the native approach:

const controller = new AbortController();
const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 30_000);try {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
  clearTimeout(timer);
  return await res.json();
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') {
    throw new Error('External API timed out after 30s');
  }
  throw err;
}

If you’re using Axios across the codebase, setting a global default is simpler:

axios.defaults.timeout = 30_000;

Thirty seconds is a reasonable ceiling for most external calls. If you know a particular endpoint typically responds in under 500 ms, set it to 2–3 seconds there. A tight timeout on a fast endpoint catches problems much earlier than a generous one.

3. Your database pool is one traffic spike away from falling over

Most database client libraries open new connections on demand with no upper bound by default. Under normal traffic this is invisible. During a traffic spike the pool starts opening connections aggressively. Relational databases have a hard connection limit, typically around 100 on a small managed instance. Once that’s hit, every new connection attempt throws an error. Not a slow query error. A hard failure.

At the same time, idle connections from quieter periods keep sitting open. Each idle Postgres connection consumes around 5–10 MB of memory on the database server. Fifty idle connections is 250–500 MB just sitting there doing nothing. The same principle applies to MySQL, SQL Server, and most other relational databases.

Three settings change this significantly. The example uses Node’s pg library, but every major database client has equivalent options:

const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max: 20,                        // hard cap on open connections
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,      // close idle connections after 30s
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000, // fail fast if pool is exhausted
});

pool.on('connect', client => {
  client.query('SET statement_timeout = 10000'); // kill queries running over 10s
});

The statement_timeout is the underrated one. Without it, a slow query from a bad filter or a missing index can hold a connection for minutes while everything queues up behind it. With it, the query gets killed and the connection is released, so your app returns an error instead of silently degrading. Most databases support an equivalent setting at the session or connection level.

For sizing the connection cap: take your database’s maximum allowed connections, divide by the number of app instances running, and leave 20–30% headroom for migrations, admin queries, and monitoring tools.

4. Your secrets are stale until you redeploy

If you’re calling a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager) once at startup with no caching, you’ve introduced a hidden operational dependency: whenever a secret rotates (a database password, an API key, a signing secret), you need to redeploy the app to pick it up. On a fast deployment pipeline that might just be annoying. On a slower one, it’s a gap where your app is running on a credential that’s already been marked as rotated.

If you’re fetching per-request instead, the problem is different but worse: 5–50 ms of latency added to every single API call, and secrets manager API costs accumulating quietly in your cloud bill.

The solution is a stale-while-revalidate cache. Serve from memory always. In the background, as the cached value approaches its TTL, fetch a fresh copy so that by the time the old one expires, the new value is already ready:

const { SecretsManagerClient, GetSecretValueCommand } = require('@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager');const client = new SecretsManagerClient({});
const cache = new Map();
const TTL = 60 * 60 * 1000; // 1 hour

async function getSecret(name) {
  const cached = cache.get(name);
  if (cached && Date.now() - cached.fetchedAt < TTL) {
    // Background refresh in the last 5 minutes of the TTL window
    if (Date.now() - cached.fetchedAt > TTL - 300_000) {
      refreshSecret(name); // intentionally not awaited
    }
    return cached.value;
  }
  return refreshSecret(name);

async function refreshSecret(name) {
  const { SecretString } = await client.send(
    new GetSecretValueCommand({ SecretId: name })
  );
  cache.set(name, { value: SecretString, fetchedAt: Date.now() });
  return SecretString;

module.exports = { getSecret };

With this in place, secret rotation takes effect within one hour automatically, with no deployment, no downtime, and no latency cost on any individual request.

This matters even more in Kubernetes or ECS. Both platforms inject secrets as environment variables at startup time, which means rotation still requires a pod restart or a new task deployment to take effect. The in-process cache sidesteps that entirely: the app fetches directly from the secrets manager at runtime, so the platform’s injection mechanism is irrelevant. The secret updates itself.

5. Nothing is stopping someone from hammering your expensive endpoints

It rarely starts maliciously. A misconfigured mobile client starts polling /search every 500 ms because someone forgot to debounce. An accidental infinite retry loop hammers /auth/login. A competitor's scraper finds your public API and decides to index everything. None of these require bad intent, and they're common enough that the question isn't whether it'll happen but when. Without rate limiting, all of that load goes straight to your database. The first sign something's wrong is your DB CPU spiking and legitimate users getting slow responses.

The important thing is thinking about rate limiting in tiers rather than as a single global rule. A blanket 200 req/15 min limit is fine for general API traffic, but authentication endpoints deserve much stricter treatment. They’re the primary target for credential stuffing attacks and brute force attempts, and each login attempt hits your database plus potentially an expensive password hash comparison. Upload endpoints similarly: each hit triggers storage I/O, processing, and database writes. Those need their own tighter limits.

In Node.js with Express, express-rate-limit handles this with minimal setup:

const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit');

// Global baseline, covers all routes
app.use(rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  max: 200,
  standardHeaders: true, // sends RateLimit-* headers to clients
  legacyHeaders: false,
}))

// Auth endpoints, strict for DDoS and brute-force prevention
const authLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  max: 10, // 10 login attempts per 15 minutes per IP
  message: 'Too many login attempts. Please try again later.',
})

// Upload endpoints, protect against storage abuse
const uploadLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 60 * 1000,
  max: 5,
});

app.post('/auth/login',    authLimiter,   loginHandler);
app.post('/auth/register', authLimiter,   registerHandler);
app.post('/upload',        uploadLimiter, uploadHandler);

The standardHeaders: true option sends RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, and RateLimit-Reset headers back to clients, which matters for legitimate API consumers who want to implement their own backoff logic. If you're running multiple app instances behind a load balancer or in a Kubernetes cluster, the default in-memory store tracks counters per instance rather than globally. An attacker spreading requests across instances effectively multiplies their limit by your instance count. Sharing state via Redis closes that gap.

Worth being clear about what this protects: rate limiting at the application layer is not a substitute for infrastructure-level DDoS protection. For high-volume attacks at thousands of requests per second, you need something upstream: AWS Shield, Cloudflare, or at minimum an ALB with WAF rules. What application-level rate limiting handles is the long tail of abuse that infrastructure tools don’t catch: subtle API misuse, accidental hammering, slow credential stuffing. Both layers together give you real coverage.

The common thread

None of these require a rewrite, a new infrastructure component, or a week of engineering time. The pattern is the same across all five: something harmless at low traffic becomes a quiet tax at scale, on latency, on cost, on resilience. Pick the ones that match where your pain is and ship them.

Before you go:

👏 If this article was useful, consider giving it a clap.

✍️ Follow for future articles on backend engineering, cloud infrastructure, performance, and system design.

📚 Explore my other articles for more practical engineering lessons and real-world examples.

item.title: AI Doesn’t Replace People. It Replaces Skill Gaps
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: For my whole career, a missing skill had one fix: learn it. AI quietly added a second option — operate competently in a domain you never mastered. That’s useful and a little unsettling. It doesn’t make expertise worthless. It changes the economics of being a non-expert.

The old rule

If you were weak at writing, you learned writing. Weak at sales, you learned sales. The gap was a debt, and study was the only honorable way to pay it.

I’ve spent 20+ years in tech. Sales and prospecting were never my strength. I understood why they mattered; I just never built the skill. For years that was fine — someone else owned that work.

The moment it broke

Then I started building something small of my own, and the protection disappeared. I suddenly needed to find leads, research companies, identify contacts, write outreach, and manage follow-ups — the exact work I’d spent two decades avoiding.

The old rule said: spend months getting good at sales.

I didn’t. I built an AI system to help me do it instead.

The part that surprised me

It wasn’t the time saved. It was that the system let me operate in a domain where I had zero confidence and no track record. I wasn’t faster at something I was already good at. I was suddenly functional at something I’d quietly decided I was bad at.

That raised a question I still can’t fully answer: are we entering a period where you no longer have to master every skill your work requires?

I started seeing it everywhere. A developer who can’t write produces useful docs. A founder with no design training gets a layout that looks intentional. A manager who dreads writing drafts the hard message instead of freezing. Someone with no stats background explores a dataset and notices real patterns.

None of them became experts. That’s the point. They became capable enough to keep moving.

The trade-offs (this is the important part)

The easy reading is “barriers are falling.” True, but incomplete. A few things are true at once:

  • The barrier to entry dropped. Work that needed a specialist is now within reach of a motivated generalist.
  • For people who do want to learn, AI accelerates it. The same tool that lets you skip the skill can teach it faster — if you’re paying attention.
  • The expert still wins. My AI-assisted outreach was good enough to function. It was not as good as a skilled salesperson’s. The gap between competent and excellent didn’t vanish. It just stopped being the gap between participating and shut out entirely. Those are very different gaps.
  • Judgment matters more, not less. When producing output costs nearly nothing, the scarce skill is knowing whether the output is any good and pointed at the right problem. AI gave me dozens of messages. It didn’t give me the judgment to know which prospects were worth pursuing.
  • Understanding the problem stays essential. The tool could execute. It couldn’t decide what I was trying to accomplish. When I was clear, it was useful. When I was vague, it produced confident nonsense.

So I think of these tools as multipliers, not substitutes. A multiplier does nothing to zero. Bring real judgment and it amplifies you. Bring none and it amplifies that too — and the result can look competent while being quietly wrong. That’s the real risk: not that weak work looks strong, but that the difference gets harder to see from the outside.

What I keep coming back to

For most of history, your reach was capped by your weakest necessary skill. The things you couldn’t do defined the edges of what you could attempt. That shaped my career — I avoided whole kinds of work because of one skill I never built.

Maybe the biggest thing AI does isn’t replacing the work people do well. Maybe it’s removing the ceiling our weakest skills used to put on what we could attempt at all.

Which leaves the question I can’t put down: when you no longer have to be good at everything your work requires, what do you choose to actually master — and how do you tell the gaps you should close from the ones you’re now free to leave open?

AI Doesn’t Replace People. It Replaces Skill Gaps was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Part 2: Advanced Features in MassTransit Mediator: Pipeline Behaviors
item.content:encoded:
In Part 1 of our series, we established the basic CQRS and automatic handler registration infrastructure using the MassTransit In-Memory Mediator.

In this second part of the series, we will cover Pipe Filters, the MassTransit counterpart of MediatR’s Pipeline Behaviors which is essential for managing cross-cutting concerns in enterprise projects.

In software engineering, cross-cutting concerns are aspects of a program that affect multiple modules or layers and cannot be cleanly separated from the rest of the system. They represent parts of the logic that “cut across” the traditional boundaries of your application’s architecture.

For instance, Global Exception Handling structures developed to catch all potential errors resulting from a user request in a single, centralized location — perfectly fit this definition. Similarly, managing the logging of all incoming requests and outgoing API responses in one place, or handling validation errors centrally, also fits this definition.

Cleaning user input (such as trimming whitespace from the beginning and end or sanitizing it from harmful characters) is another example that falls under this concept, and this process is called sanitization.

In MediatR or similar packages, we would write Behaviors for this purpose. We can, of course, achieve this with MassTransit as well, where it is referred to as MassTransit Filters. Here, we will develop two filters together. By doing so, we will provide useful and directly applicable examples while explaining our main topic. The first of these examples will be building a centralized logging mechanism, and the second will be establishing a central validation structure utilizing FluentValidation, a validation library most of us are already familiar with.

1. Pipeline Behaviors (MassTransit Pipe Filters)

MassTransit provides a highly advanced pipeline structure for customizing the message processing pipeline. We can create our custom filters by implementing the IFilter<ConsumeContext<T>> interface.

In this phase, we will examine 2 basic filters for logging and validation. However, MassTransit allows developers to add and run many filters sequentially according to their needs.

A. Logging Filter

Let’s develop a filter that tracks the start and end times of requests and logs errors.

First, let’s create a simple ILoggable interface to mark the requests we want to log and to mask sensitive data:

public interface ILoggable
{
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object?> BuildLogData();
}

Next, with the filter below, we can log how long a request took to process along with the request-response payload and elapsed time information. This logging operation will occur if the LogLevel.Information level is enabled in the application settings:

using MassTransit;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text.Json;

public class LoggingFilter<T>(ILogger<LoggingFilter<T>> logger) 
    : IFilter<ConsumeContext<T>> where T : class
{
    public async Task Send(ConsumeContext<T> context, IPipe<ConsumeContext<T>> next)
    {
        var requestName = typeof(T).Name;
        var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        // Request logging (checks the logging interface to mask sensitive data if applicable)
        if (context.Message is ILoggable loggableRequest)
        {
            if (logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Information))
            {
                string logData = JsonSerializer.Serialize(loggableRequest.BuildLogData());
                logger.LogInformation("Handling {RequestName} with payload {Request}", requestName, logData);
            }
        }
        try
        {
            await next.Send(context); // Forward the flow to the next filter or Handler
            stopwatch.Stop();
            logger.LogInformation("{RequestName} completed successfully in {Elapsed}ms", requestName, stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds);
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            stopwatch.Stop();
            logger.LogError(ex, "{RequestName} failed in {Elapsed}ms", requestName, stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds);
            throw; // Rethrow the exception so that the Global Exception Handler can catch it
        }
    }
    public void Probe(ProbeContext context) => context.CreateFilterScope("logging");
}

B. Validation Filter

We can intercept requests before they are processed to perform validation checks and return to the user without processing the request if there is a validation error. The following filter, which integrates the FluentValidation library into the pipeline, will serve this purpose.

Error Management Note: When you catch MassTransit errors inside a global exception handler, the error is wrapped in a MassTransit.RequestException.
To access the actual exception (for example, the ValidationException thrown by FluentValidation), you can perform the following check in your exception-catching blocks:
if (exception is MassTransit.RequestException && exception.InnerException != null) 
{     
  exception = exception.InnerException; 
}
using FluentValidation;
using MassTransit;

public class ValidationFilter<T>(IEnumerable<IValidator<T>> validators) 
    : IFilter<ConsumeContext<T>> where T : class
{
    public async Task Send(ConsumeContext<T> context, IPipe<ConsumeContext<T>> next)
    {
        if (validators.Any())
        {
            var validationContext = new ValidationContext<T>(context.Message);
            var validationResults = await Task.WhenAll(
                validators.Select(v => v.ValidateAsync(validationContext, context.CancellationToken))
            );
            
            var failures = validationResults
                .SelectMany(r => r.Errors)
                .Where(f => f != null)
                .ToList();
            if (failures.Count != 0)
                throw new ValidationException(failures);
        }
        await next.Send(context);
    }
    public void Probe(ProbeContext context) => context.CreateFilterScope("validation");
}

2. Registering Filters to MassTransit Mediator

To ensure our filters execute in order, we update the AddMediator configuration in ServiceRegistration.cs. Filters will be triggered in the order they are added:

services.AddMediator(cfg =>
{
    // Scanning and adding handlers
    cfg.AddConsumers(consumerTypes);
    // Pipeline Filter Ordering (MediatR Behaviors Counterpart)
    cfg.ConfigureMediator((context, mediatorCfg) =>
    {
        // First data is validated and finally the action is logged.
        mediatorCfg.UseConsumeFilter(typeof(ValidationFilter<>), context);
        mediatorCfg.UseConsumeFilter(typeof(LoggingFilter<>), context);
    });
});

In Summary, What Did We Gain?

By migrating from MediatR to MassTransit’s In-Memory Mediator and leveraging its advanced middleware pipeline, we achieve several major architectural benefits:

No More MediatR Dependency (Licensing & Future-proofing):

  • Cost & Compliance: We transitioned away from MediatR, removing any potential licensing, commercial usage, or organizational restrictions. By adopting MassTransit — a fully free, open-source framework under the Apache 2.0 license — we ensure that our core messaging infrastructure remains open and cost-effective forever.
  • Community & Ecosystem: MassTransit is backed by an incredibly active community and a mature ecosystem that is heavily maintained. Instead of using a tool solely focused on in-memory dispatching, we get a production-ready messaging platform designed for scale.

Powerful and Flexible Pipeline (Advanced Middleware):

  • A True Pipes-and-Filters Architecture: Unlike MediatR’s pipeline behaviors, which can sometimes feel rigid or harder to debug, MassTransit uses a highly optimized greenfield pipeline architecture (GreenPipes).
  • Flexible Execution & Ordering: We can inject cross-cutting concerns (such as sanitization, schema validation, and request logging) with explicit control over their execution order. Filters can inspect, mutate, or short-circuit messages before they ever reach the target handlers.
  • Granular Control: Since MassTransit exposes the ConsumeContext<T>, we get direct access to message metadata, headers, cancellation tokens, and scope-specific dependency injection out of the box.

Microservices Ready (Zero-friction Distributed Scaling):

  • Decoupled Architecture: This is perhaps the greatest advantage. In a traditional MediatR setup, if you decide to extract a handler into a separate microservice, you are forced to rewrite your dispatching code, introduce HTTP/gRPC clients, or manually integrate a message broker.
  • Simple Configuration Switch: With MassTransit, your application logic is written using consumers (IConsumer<T>). If you decide to transition from an in-memory mediator to a distributed broker (such as RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, or Amazon SQS), you do not need to modify a single line of your business logic (Handlers). You simply swap out the AddMediator configuration in your Dependency Injection bootstrap (ServiceRegistration.cs) with a bus configuration (e.g., UsingRabbitMq). The transport change is completely transparent to the rest of the application.

Frankly, based on my research, I can also say that MediatR is faster than MassTransit. At its core, it is a very lightweight In-Memory router. When it receives a request, it resolves the corresponding IRequestHandler from the dependency injection (DI) container and calls the method directly. There is no extra layer of abstraction in between; the process simply consists of a direct synchronous or asynchronous method call.

On the other hand, the MassTransit In-Memory Mediator structure is a scaled-down, in-memory version of MassTransit’s full-fledged Service Bus architecture. When you send a message, MassTransit passes it through a pipeline. Filters, scoped object management, logging mechanisms, and serialization/automation steps (even if optional) run on this pipeline. Of course, you can achieve this with MediatR Behaviors as well, but MassTransit Mediator runs slightly slower compared to MediatR.

However, this latency is just a drop in the ocean compared to the duration of a single async request your application would make to a database or an external API. Additionally, MediatR remains slightly more performant in terms of memory footprint.

That being said, apart from resolving all licensing issues, MassTransit brings advanced features that you can utilize throughout the entire project, such as Automatic Retry, Outbox, Saga, and Rate Limiting. For instance, it can even replace libraries like Polly, which we all know and use.

Part 2: Advanced Features in MassTransit Mediator: Pipeline Behaviors was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Vector Search, Explained Visually — How Databases Find a Needle in 5 Million Vectors
item.content:encoded:
Five Million Items, One Aisle

You’ve embedded your documents. Five million chunks, each one now a vector — a point on a meaning-map. A question arrives, also a vector. All you have to do is find its closest neighbors.

Out of five million. Per query. Fast.

Here’s the whole problem, and the whole solution, as a supermarket.

Imagine a supermarket with no shelves. Every product the store sells, dumped in one giant random pile on the floor. You want milk? Start picking things up. One at a time. Item 4,999,997: dog food. Nope.

That’s brute-force vector search — a linear scan. It always finds the true nearest match. It just dies at scale.

And it’s not one shopper. Every query re-checks the entire pile. A corner shop can live like this — a few thousand vectors and brute force is actually instant, and you should genuinely just do that. Five million items with a queue at the door? The pile is on fire.

Real shops solved this centuries ago: aisles. You walk to dairy and ignore the other forty. Thirty items checked instead of thirty thousand.

Notice what actually happened there. You didn’t get faster at checking. You got better at not looking.

But there’s a catch, and it’s the most honest thing about this whole field: the oat milk was shelved in DRINKS. You opened dairy. You missed it.

That’s the “Approximate” in ANN — Approximate Nearest Neighbour search. You accept “usually finds the best match” in exchange for “done in a heartbeat.” There’s no free lunch; there’s a dial. (Researchers proved the trade-off is fundamental back in 1998 — in high dimensions, the exact shortcuts collapse.)

Hold this one picture for everything that follows: random pile = check everything. Aisles = open only the one you need. Every vector-search concept you’ll ever meet is just a detail of how aisles get built and how many you open.

So how do five million items get sorted into aisles? Nobody sorts them. The store sorts itself: similar vectors clump, you draw a boundary around each clump, and you plant a signpost at its centre — the average position of everything inside (a centroid).

And here’s the mechanism, free of charge — the two-step that saves five million checks:

  1. Compare the query against a handful of signposts (one per aisle).
  2. Open only the nearest aisle and scan its few thousand items.

Everything else? Never looked at. That’s the entire trick. In FAISS — the famous search library — this shelving method is called IVF, and “how many aisles to open” is the knob named nprobe.

Because here’s where it gets expensive in real life: you’ve mastered the clever shelving. Now try to run a shop with nothing but shelves.

Who restocks while the store is open? Who remembers the stock after the lights go out? Who handles “search by meaning — but only THIS customer’s documents”?

That last one — the metadata filter — is the quietly crucial feature real apps need constantly, and a bare search algorithm simply cannot do it. The difference between the shelving trick and a vector database is the difference between a shelving method and an actual running supermarket with staff, a stockroom, and a returns desk.

The full episode covers what the preview deliberately doesn’t:

  • what a vector database adds on top of ANN (persistence, live updates, filters, hybrid search) — and why FAISS is a library, not a database
  • why filters fight the aisles (“filtered ANN” is genuinely hard, and every DB solves it differently)
  • the history twist: vector databases predate ChatGPT by years
  • who actually does the searching in RAG (spoiler: the LLM finds nothing), and how that tells you exactly what to fix when answers go wrong
  • a clickable sources page — every claim checked, no hand-waving

item.title: GRPO in Production: The Failure Modes Nobody Writes About
item.content:encoded:
GRPO is now the default RL algorithm for post-training LLMs. DeepSeek-R1 popularized it, and it’s since been adopted in Nemotron 3 Super, Qwen-Math derivatives, and dozens of open-source reasoning models. The explainer posts that followed all show the happy path: sample G responses per prompt, compute group-relative advantages, update the policy. Clean, elegant, cheaper than PPO because there’s no critic network.

What those posts don’t show is what happens at step 400 when your training loss goes flat, your rewards stop improving, and your model starts generating increasingly confident, increasingly wrong outputs. This is a post about those moments.

TL;DR

  • GRPO’s group-relative advantage computation has three silent failure modes: entropy collapse, advantage collapse, and KL drift.
  • Advantage collapse is the most common and the least diagnosed — it happens whenever your rollout group returns uniform rewards, which is most of the time on hard prompts.
  • DAPO (Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization) addresses all three with concrete algorithmic fixes you can apply to any GRPO training loop today.
  • Monitoring entropy and advantage variance as first-class training metrics is not optional at production scale.

What GRPO Actually Does

GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, introduced by DeepSeek in DeepSeekMath) is a policy gradient algorithm that gets rid of the critic model PPO requires. Instead of a learned value function estimating expected return, it estimates advantages by comparing responses within a sampled group.

For each prompt q, you sample G responses {y_1, ..., y_G} from the current policy π_θ, compute a scalar reward R_i for each, then normalize:

Â_i = (R_i - mean(R)) / std(R)

The policy is then updated to increase the probability of high-advantage responses and decrease low-advantage ones, subject to a KL penalty against a frozen reference model π_ref.

In PyTorch, the core training step looks roughly like this:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def grpo_loss(
    log_probs: torch.Tensor,       # [G, seq_len] - current policy log probs
    old_log_probs: torch.Tensor,   # [G, seq_len] - log probs from rollout
    rewards: torch.Tensor,         # [G] - scalar rewards per response
    ref_log_probs: torch.Tensor,   # [G, seq_len] - reference model log probs
    epsilon: float = 0.2,
    beta: float = 0.04,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Group-relative advantage: normalize within the sampled group
    advantages = (rewards - rewards.mean()) / (rewards.std() + 1e-8)
    advantages = advantages.unsqueeze(1)  # broadcast over sequence
    # PPO-style clipped surrogate objective
    ratio = torch.exp(log_probs - old_log_probs)
    clipped = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - epsilon, 1 + epsilon)
    policy_loss = -torch.min(ratio * advantages, clipped * advantages).mean()
    # KL penalty against reference model
    kl_div = (old_log_probs - ref_log_probs).mean()
    
    return policy_loss + beta * kl_div

This is clean. On math benchmarks with binary rewards (correct/incorrect), GRPO produces strong results — and eliminates the memory overhead of a value network, cutting training compute nearly in half versus PPO.

The problem is that this advantage formulation has sharp edges when your reward distribution stops cooperating.

Failure Mode 1: Advantage Collapse

This is the silent killer. It happens whenever all G responses in a group receive the same reward.

When std(R) ≈ 0the denominator Â_i = (R_i - mean(R)) / std(R) approaches zero. The 1e-8 The epsilon you add prevents a NaN, but what you get instead is a near-zero advantage for every response in the group. Zero advantage means zero gradient signal. The policy doesn't update. Training stalls.

When does this happen? Far more often than the GRPO paper implies:

  • Hard prompts: On genuinely difficult reasoning tasks, all G rollouts get reward = 0. No correct answer in the group means no contrast to learn from.
  • Easy prompts: All G rollouts get a reward = 1. The model has already solved these — again, no contrast.

As your model improves, the distribution of “easy” prompts grows. As you push into harder domains, the “impossible” set grows. You end up with a dumbbell distribution — and GRPO is starved of gradient signal at both ends.

def diagnose_advantage_collapse(rewards_per_group: list[torch.Tensor]) -> dict:
    """
    Track the fraction of groups where advantage collapse occurs.
    Log this every N steps during training.
    """
    collapsed = 0
    for group_rewards in rewards_per_group:
        if group_rewards.std() < 1e-4:
            collapsed += 1
    
    collapse_rate = collapsed / len(rewards_per_group)
    return {
        "advantage_collapse_rate": collapse_rate,
        # If this exceeds 0.3, your training is stalling. Act immediately.
    }

DAPO’s fix: dynamic sampling. Filter out groups where all responses are correct or all are incorrect before computing the loss. Only train on groups with actual reward variance. This feels aggressive — you’re discarding a significant fraction of your rollout compute — but the alternative is updating the policy on noise.

Failure Mode 2: Entropy Collapse

Entropy collapse is slower-acting and harder to detect because your reward metrics can look fine while it’s happening.

As training progresses, the policy naturally concentrates probability mass on high-reward responses. This is the point of RL. But if entropy drops too fast, the policy loses diversity in its generations. You end up with a model that produces a narrow set of responses — and because GRPO’s group advantage is relative, a group of similar low-diversity responses gives you a similarly weak gradient signal.

Worse: once entropy collapses, it tends to stay collapsed. The policy has committed to a mode. Recovery requires either re-annealing the KL penalty or external injection of diversity.

def token_entropy(log_probs: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    """
    Compute mean per-token entropy across a batch.
    Healthy range during early training: > 2.0 nats.
    Alert threshold: < 0.5 nats sustained for > 50 steps.
    """
    probs = log_probs.exp()
    entropy = -(probs * log_probs).sum(dim=-1).mean()
    return entropy.item()

DAPO’s fix: an asymmetric KL clip. Standard GRPO clips the probability ratio symmetrically at [1-ε, 1+ε]. DAPO uses [1-ε_low, 1+ε_high] with ε_high > ε_low — loosening the upper bound. This allows the policy to increase the probability of correct responses more aggressively, which counterintuitively preserves entropy because the model doesn't need to compress its output distribution as hard to capture the reward signal. More headroom means less pressure to collapse.

Failure Mode 3: KL Drift

The KL penalty in GRPO is meant to keep the updated policy close to the reference model (usually the SFT checkpoint you started from). In practice, the penalty coefficient β is a blunt instrument.

Set β too low and the policy drifts fast — you get reward hacking, degenerate outputs, and loss of the format and calibration that SFT gave you. Set it too high, and the penalty dominates the training signal — you're paying KL cost to stay close to a reference that's weaker than what you're trying to train toward. The model stops improving.

The standard approach of adding KL as a reward penalty (r_effective = r - β * KL(π || π_ref)) compounds this: you're shaping the reward signal itself, which interacts badly with group normalization. A group where one response has unusually high KL gets penalized in the reward, then again in the loss.

# STANDARD (problematic at scale):
kl_penalty = beta * (current_log_prob - ref_log_prob)
adjusted_reward = reward - kl_penalty  # KL baked into reward signal
# DAPO-STYLE (cleaner):
# Remove KL from the reward entirely.
# Apply it as a direct loss term after advantage computation.
# This decouples exploration pressure from reward normalization.
policy_loss = grpo_surrogate(log_probs, advantages)
kl_loss = F.kl_div(log_probs, ref_log_probs, reduction='batchmean', log_target=True)
total_loss = policy_loss + beta * kl_loss

Decoupling KL from the reward lets you tune β on the loss side without distorting the reward distribution that advantage normalization depends on.

Failure Mode 4 (Bonus): Token-Level vs. Sample-Level Loss Normalization

This one is subtle but materially affects the reasoning model quality. Standard GRPO normalizes loss at the sample level — each response contributes equally to the gradient regardless of length.

This creates a structural bias against long chain-of-thought responses. A 2000-token reasoning trace is treated the same as a 200-token direct answer in terms of gradient weight. If the longer trace is what produced the correct answer, you’re underweighting the exact behavior you want to reinforce.

Token-level normalization, introduced in DAPO, divides the loss by the total number of tokens in the group rather than the number of responses:

def token_level_loss(
    log_probs: torch.Tensor,      # [G, seq_len]
    advantages: torch.Tensor,     # [G, seq_len] — broadcast from [G]
    attention_mask: torch.Tensor, # [G, seq_len] — 1 for real tokens, 0 for padding
) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Per-token policy loss
    per_token_loss = -log_probs * advantages * attention_mask
    
    # Normalize by total token count, not response count
    total_tokens = attention_mask.sum()
    return per_token_loss.sum() / total_tokens

On math reasoning benchmarks, DAPO’s final configuration (50 AIME points) outperformed DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B (47 points) using 50% fewer training steps. Token-level normalization was one of the key contributors — not a minor tweak.

Gotchas: What Nobody Tells You

1. Your reward model is probably the real bottleneck, not GRPO.

All three GRPO failure modes are amplified by noisy rewards. If your verifier misclassifies 15% of responses, you’re injecting a false signal into every group. Advantage collapse gets worse because “hard” prompts, where the model is near threshold, flip between all-correct and all-incorrect groups unpredictably. Audit your reward model before diagnosing your training loop.

2. GRPO failure modes compound across training stages.

Entropy collapse in stage 1 (SFT warm-start) creates a fragile starting point that makes advantage collapse more likely in stage 2 (RL fine-tuning). Teams that report “GRPO didn’t work for us” often ran it on an SFT checkpoint that was already over-fitted to a narrow response format. Check the entropy of your SFT model before you start RL.

3. The G hyperparameter interacts non-linearly with all three failure modes.

Increasing group size G reduces variance in advantage estimates and reduces collapse frequency — but also increases rollout cost linearly. Most production setups use G=8 or G=16. Going to G=32 can rescue a training run that's stuck, but the cost may not be worth it when dynamic sampling (dropping bad groups) achieves the same result at lower compute.

Conclusion

GRPO is genuinely a better default than PPO for LLM post-training: lower memory, comparable or better results, no critic. But the framing of “simpler than PPO” has led teams to underestimate its failure modes. Advantage collapse is structural — it’s not a bug you fix, it’s a property of group-relative normalization that you have to engineer around. Entropy collapse is slow and invisible until your loss curves look healthy, but your model has stopped generalizing.

The DAPO paper (Yu et al., 2025) is the most important engineering document in post-training right now, not because it’s theoretically novel, but because it maps each failure mode to a concrete fix: dynamic sampling, token-level normalization, asymmetric clip, and decoupled KL. You don’t have to adopt all of them. But you should understand all of them — because your training run will hit at least one.

The next frontier is agentic RL: multi-step tool-calling trajectories where reward is sparse, rollouts are expensive, and the assumption of “verifiable correct/incorrect” breaks down entirely. The failure modes are the same, just harder to detect. That’s a post for another day.
